summary: Ornidazole is a 5-nitroimidazole antimicrobial active against anaerobic bacteria and protozoa, used for amoebiasis, giardiasis, trichomoniasis, bacterial vaginosis, anaerobic infections, and surgical prophylaxis against anaerobes. Compared with metronidazole it has a longer half-life (~13 hours), allowing less frequent dosing, and is reported to have a milder alcohol (disulfiram-like) interaction. It is NOT FDA-approved; it is widely licensed in Europe, India, and other regions (SmPC/regional labelling).
indications: Prophylaxis of post-operative anaerobic infection (e.g., colorectal/gynaecological surgery)

moa: Ornidazole is a 5-nitroimidazole prodrug. After entering anaerobic bacteria and protozoa, its nitro group is reduced by intracellular electron-transport proteins to reactive nitro radicals that bind and damage DNA, causing strand breakage and inhibition of nucleic-acid synthesis, leading to cell death. The reduction occurs efficiently only under the low redox conditions found in anaerobes and protozoa, accounting for its selectivity.

absolute: Known hypersensitivity to ornidazole or other nitroimidazoles
monitor: Neurological status (peripheral neuropathy, seizures) with prolonged or high-dose therapy

preg: Avoid during the first trimester. Use during pregnancy only if clearly essential and the benefit outweighs the potential risk, in line with regional labelling. Nitroimidazoles cross the placenta.
lact: Ornidazole is excreted in breast milk. Avoid breastfeeding during treatment, or temporarily discontinue nursing.
renal: No major dose adjustment is generally required; use with caution in severe renal impairment. Ornidazole and metabolites are partly removed by dialysis.
hepatic: In severe hepatic impairment the elimination half-life is prolonged; double the dosing interval (reduce dosing frequency) and monitor.

major: Oral anticoagulants (warfarin/coumarins) — ornidazole may enhance anticoagulant effect; monitor INR and adjust dose
moderate: Vecuronium and other muscle relaxants — prolonged neuromuscular blockade
Drugs lowering seizure threshold / CNS-active agents — caution with neurotoxicity
interactions.food: Take with food to reduce gastrointestinal upset.
interactions.alcohol: Avoid alcohol as a precaution; ornidazole does not inhibit aldehyde dehydrogenase to the same degree as metronidazole, so the disulfiram-like reaction is reported to be milder/absent, but caution is advised.
interactions.diagnostics: No specific laboratory test interference of note.

pearls: NOT FDA-approved — licensed in EU (SmPC), India and many other regions; this record is based on SmPC/BNF-type sources, not an FDA label
Longer half-life (~13 h) than metronidazole allows less frequent dosing and convenient single-dose regimens
Milder/absent disulfiram-like alcohol reaction compared with metronidazole, but alcohol avoidance is still commonly advised

missed: Take the missed dose as soon as remembered. If it is nearly time for the next dose, skip the missed dose. Do not double the dose.
overdose: Overdose may cause exaggerated adverse effects, particularly neurological (seizures, peripheral neuropathy) and gastrointestinal symptoms. There is no specific antidote; manage with supportive and symptomatic care (diazepam for seizures). Dialysis can remove ornidazole if needed.
